summary: Describes the BEEP core, a generic application protocol kernel for connection-oriented, asynchronous interactions. It provides framing and multiplexing so new application protocols can be built on top. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: BEEP is a core for connection-oriented applications that need to exchange messages asynchronously. It handles message framing, independent channels and profile negotiation, while application designers define the messages for their own task.

subtitle: A reusable application protocol core for framing messages, managing channels and negotiating profiles.

tldr.problem: Application protocols that use a connection need common mechanisms for framing messages, handling concurrent exchanges and negotiating security or authentication.
tldr.mechanism: BEEP frames MIME messages and carries independent exchanges on numbered channels in one session. Channel zero manages channels, each of which uses an agreed profile.
tldr.outcome: Protocol designers can define application-specific profiles while reusing the BEEP core. RFC 3080 is a Proposed Standard and leaves the transport mapping to separate documents.

today: RFC 3080 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2001. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; transport bindings are specified separately, including TCP mapping in RFC 3081.

sections.title: The BEEP Protocol Core
sections.content:
BEEP (Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol) is a generic application protocol kernel for connection-oriented, asynchronous interactions. Its framing mechanism supports simultaneous, independent message exchanges between peers in one session.

Messages contain MIME content and are exchanged on channels. Each channel binds a well-defined part of the application, such as data exchange, authentication or transport security, and has a profile that defines its messages and their meaning. This RFC defines channel management, a TLS profile and a family of SASL profiles; other application profiles are defined separately.
sections.plainLanguage: BEEP provides shared connection and message-handling rules for applications. Each channel has a profile that defines the purpose and meaning of messages sent on it.

sections.title: Peers, Roles and Exchange Styles
sections.content:
BEEP is peer-to-peer, but it uses two pairs of role names. The peer waiting for a connection is the listener; the peer opening it is the initiator. For an exchange, the peer that starts the message is the client and the other is the server. These roles do not have to match the connection roles.

BEEP defines three exchange styles. MSG/RPY is a request followed by a positive reply. MSG/ERR is a request followed by a negative reply. In MSG/ANS, the server sends zero or more answers and ends the response with NUL.
sections.plainLanguage: Either peer can start an exchange, even though one peer opened the connection. A request receives one positive reply, one negative reply, or a set of answers followed by an end marker.

sections.title: Messages, Frames and Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
A BEEP message follows MIME rules and may contain text or binary content. It is normally sent in one frame, but can be split across several. Each frame has a printable-ASCII header, a payload and an END trailer; the header identifies the message type, channel, message number, continuation state, sequence number and payload size.

A continuation indicator tells the receiver whether further frames follow or the message is complete. Sequence numbers count payload octets on each channel and wrap in their defined 32-bit sequence-number space. Frames of a segmented message stay in sequence on their channel, while frames on other channels can be interleaved.

A malformed frame, unexpected sequence number or missing trailer terminates the session without a response. A diagnostic entry is recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: Each frame labels its channel, message and position in the data stream. The labels let a receiver put message parts in order and detect missing or malformed frames.

sections.title: Channel Zero Manages the Session
sections.content:
When a session starts, only channel 0 exists. It carries channel-management messages: peers greet each other and advertise supported profiles, create channels with start, and close channels or release the session with close. A peer should support at least 257 concurrent channels.

Initiating peers choose odd channel numbers and listening peers choose even channel numbers. A profile can include an initialization message of at most 4K octets. The receiving peer accepts one proposed profile or returns an error. A three-digit reply code provides a machine-readable result.
sections.plainLanguage: Channel zero handles setup and changes to the session. Peers use it to agree on a profile, open a numbered channel, or close a channel when its work is done.

sections.title: Pipelining and Parallel Channels
sections.content:
A client may send several messages on one channel before receiving their replies. The server processes and answers those messages in the order received. This is pipelining within a channel.

Different channels operate independently. A server may process their messages in any order, so BEEP does not require replies on separate channels to arrive in a particular order. In a one-to-many exchange, answer frames can also be interleaved and are associated with their answer numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can send several requests on one channel without waiting, and their replies stay in order. Work on separate channels can proceed at the same time without a shared reply order.

sections.title: Starting TLS Within a Session
sections.content:
A new BEEP session transfers data without privacy. The RFC defines a TLS transport-security profile based on TLS version one. A client requests it by starting the profile with a ready message; the other peer replies with proceed or an error.

When TLS negotiation begins, all channels, including channel zero, are implicitly closed. After the negotiation ends, both peers send new greetings. The ready exchange pauses other traffic on the underlying transport until the peer responds.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers can request TLS through a BEEP profile. Starting that negotiation closes the current channels, and both peers greet each other again after it finishes.

sections.title: Authentication with SASL Profiles
sections.content:
BEEP starts with anonymous access. The RFC defines a family of profiles based on SASL mechanisms registered with IANA. A client opens a channel for a mechanism, and the peers exchange challenges and responses in blob elements; the content is base64-encoded.

A blob status can indicate that a client aborted, a server completed authentication or the exchange should continue. Successful authentication updates the identity for all existing and future channels, and the session permits no further authentication attempts. Authorization remains the responsibility of each peer.

A SASL security layer and transport security must not both be negotiated in the same session: once one succeeds, the other security negotiation must not begin.
sections.plainLanguage: SASL profiles let peers exchange authentication challenges and responses. After authentication succeeds, the identity applies to every channel in the session, but each peer still decides which actions to allow.

sections.title: Security Depends on the Profiles
sections.content:
BEEP framing by itself does not protect a session from attack. Security comes from the TLS or SASL profiles used with it, and each channel should apply access control based on the session's authenticated identity and privacy level.

A man-in-the-middle may remove security profiles from a greeting, reject TLS setup or push the peers toward a weaker cipher suite. Peers may be configured to refuse insufficient privacy or weak suites. After a successful negotiation, a peer must discard information cached from exchanges before security was active.
sections.plainLanguage: BEEP's message framing is not encryption or authentication. Peers must negotiate a security profile, check that the negotiation is acceptable and apply access control to each channel.

items.label: Answer
items.desc: Carries one answer in a one-to-many exchange.

items.title: greeting
items.text: Advertises profiles when the session begins.

items.title: start
items.text: Requests creation of a channel for a profile.

items.title: close
items.text: Requests closure of a channel or the session.

items.title: error
items.text: Rejects a request or reports a problem.
